To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stem cell niche, the microenvironment in which the stem cells reside, is critical for maintaining stem cell function and that this microenvironment changes during wound healing and cancer.

stem cell (SC) plasticity is a process by which SCs can change their lineage outputs in response to environmental cues and that this process is regulated by a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic factors.

(1) the haematopoetic stem cell niche is a complex structure that controls stem cell fate, (2) the skin epitheliam niche is a complex and dynamic structure that controls stem cells and (3) the intestinal epitheliam niche consists of a complex network of signalling molecules and cells that controls stem cell function and fate
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms that control the fate of stem cells.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the maintenance of tissue-specific SC populations.
understanding the mechanisms that control the behaviour of adult stem cells and the factors that can alter their normal functions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SCs are not only able to change into different cell lineages but they are also able to change back into their original state.
SCs are the cells that are most capable of adapting to their environment.
SC plasticity is a dynamic process that is controlled by the balance of intrinsic SC and extrinsic niche factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SCs have evolved to respond to a variety of signals, including those emanating from their niche, to ensure tissue homeostasis, but also to respond to signals from damaged tissue to ensure repair.
stem cells have a plasticity, which is a property that can be exploited for tissue regeneration and cancer treatment.

the homeostasis of a tissue is governed by the interplay of multiple factors including the niche microenvironment, the intrinsic properties of the SCs, and the extrinsic signals emanating from the tissue itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SC plasticity can be harnessed to promote regeneration and prevent tumorigenesis.
SC plasticity is a dynamic process that involves multiple signalling pathways, which can be targeted to control SC behaviour.
SC plasticity is a highly dynamic, multifactorial process that involves both the SC itself and its niche.
